claims.text: All tonkatsu is coated in panko (wheat breadcrumbs) and fried in shared oil. No source documents a dedicated GF fryer or any separation of wheat-free items.
House-made dipping sauce is served alongside rock salt. The soy sauce base of the house sauce almost certainly contains wheat; no tamari or GF soy sauce alternative is mentioned in any source.
All dishes involve pork; miso soup is pork-broth based. No plant-only cooking surface or preparation area is described.
No allergy protocol, allergen menu, or staff allergy-handling practice is documented in any reviewed source. Guests with dietary restrictions should call the restaurant directly before reserving.
The reservation-only format means each order is prepared individually to order, which in principle reduces the risk of rushed cross-contamination compared to high-volume kitchens.

name: とんかつ専門店 からり (Tonkatsu Semmonten Karari)

claims.text: Tonkatsu is coated in wheat flour and panko; wheat is intrinsic to the dish, not a cross-contamination risk — it is the primary allergen present. No dedicated fryer for GF items exists or is mentioned.
No allergen breakdown is published. Standard Japanese miso soup and sauces served alongside tonkatsu routinely contain wheat-based shoyu; no GF soy sauce alternative is mentioned.
Pork is fried in the same oil used for all items including shrimp. No plant-based items are on the menu, so vegan cross-contact is moot — the menu is entirely animal-based.
No source mentions any allergy inquiry protocol or staff training in allergen handling. The restaurant does not appear to have published any allergen chart or accommodation policy.
The kitchen produces udon (pure wheat) alongside soba, making shared surfaces and water a near-certain cross-contact risk. No separation or allergen protocol has been documented.
Standard Japanese soba tsuyu is made with soy sauce that contains wheat. No tamari or wheat-free soy sauce alternative has been reported for this establishment.
Katsuo (bonito) dashi is the expected base for all soba broth and tsuyu here; no plant-based broth option is documented. Fish-stock contact unavoidable.
No allergy-handling protocol, allergen menu, or English allergy communication has been documented at this restaurant. Inquire directly in Japanese before ordering.

Soba is freshly hand-pulled on premises from local Nagano buckwheat flour — if the noodle ratio and sauce ingredients can be confirmed, there is a potential path for a gluten-sensitive (non-celiac) diner eating plain cold soba without tsuyu.

name: 山の間 (Yamanoma Brewery & Craft Beer Pub)

claims.text: Beer contains gluten and the kitchen is a mixed pub kitchen — GF diners must ask carefully.
Local-ingredient menu with some vegan/veg options; confirm dashi/soy in each dish.
A relaxed spot near the station where a vegetarian/vegan can find a few plant-based plates alongside local craft beer.
Tempura is served at this restaurant, indicating wheat flour frying is happening in the kitchen. No information about a dedicated fryer or separation from soba preparation was found.
Traditional Japanese soba tsuyu (dipping sauce) is made with wheat-containing soy sauce (koikuchi shoyu). No tamari or gluten-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned at this restaurant.
Dashi in traditional soba broth is typically bonito-based (katsuo dashi). Duck and herring soba are on the menu. No kombu-only or vegan dashi option is advertised.
English menu and English-speaking staff reported available, which may help communicate dietary needs.

name: 善光寺 兄部坊 (Zenkoji Konokonbou)

claims.text: Hand-pulled soba is prepared and served on-site; no information about dedicated equipment or separation from wheat-containing ingredients. Soba flour itself is gluten-free but cross-contact with wheat during noodle making is a real risk in Japanese temple kitchens.
Millet wheat gluten (fu) is named as a signature ingredient in the flagship Muryoju course, meaning wheat gluten is actively cooked in the kitchen.

Standard Japanese soy sauce containing wheat is used — the menu references a 'grilled miso and spicy radish dipping sauce' (焼味噌と辛味大根つゆ) for soba, and soy sauce is a standard shojin ryori condiment. No wheat-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned.

No animal products are used in shojin ryori cooking — no meat, fish, eggs, or dairy. Buddhist culinary rules prohibit animal ingredients kitchen-wide, so cross-contact with animal products is extremely unlikely.

The official contact page notes 'menu content adjustable based on requests and budget' (料理内容はご要望・ご予算に応じて変更可能), suggesting the kitchen can accommodate some dietary modifications. Phone reservations (026-234-6677) allow for direct conversation about needs. No formal allergy protocol is documented.
Fully plant-based kitchen by centuries-old Buddhist rule — no meat, fish, eggs, dairy, or bonito dashi used in any dish. Vegan diners can eat with confidence across the entire menu.
Alliums (garlic, onion, leek, chives) are excluded from all dishes per Buddhist culinary tradition, making this suitable for diners avoiding these ingredients.

name: 善光寺表参道 たき澤 (Zenkoji Omotesando Takizawa)

claims.text: Nihan soba (wheat-containing) and juwari soba (100% buckwheat) are both made and served in the same kitchen. No source documents any separation of wheat and buckwheat preparation areas, utensils, or cooking water.
Chicken tempura (wheat batter) is a flagship menu item; dedicated fryer status is undocumented.
Standard Japanese soba tsuyu typically contains wheat-based soy sauce (醤油). No tamari or wheat-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned by any source.
Fish dashi (bonito and mackerel) is used in the soba broth. Chicken is present throughout the menu at every service period. No plant-based broth alternative is documented.
No allergy menu, allergen sheet, or staff allergy-handling protocol has been documented by any reviewed source. Phone: 026-217-2415.
Juwari soba (十割そば, 100% buckwheat) is available daily in limited quantities — wheat-free at the noodle level, subject to kitchen cross-contamination caveat.
Cards accepted (VISA, Mastercard, JCB, AMEX, Diners, Suica/IC cards, iD, QUICPay) — not cash-only.

name: 善光寺宿坊 常住院 (Zenkoji Shukubo Jojuin)

claims.text: No information on cross-contamination protocols is publicly available. The kitchen serves both shojin and non-shojin (non-vegetarian) courses, so shared kitchen equipment cannot be ruled out.

Standard shojin ryori uses conventional Japanese soy sauce (shoyu), which contains wheat. Fu (wheat gluten cake) is a classic shojin ingredient and appears commonly in such menus. No tamari or wheat-free soy sauce alternatives are mentioned in any source.
The kitchen is documented to serve non-vegetarian kaiseki courses alongside shojin options; shared preparation surfaces between courses cannot be confirmed as separate from available sources.

The Zenkoji official shukubo page notes that Jojuin accommodates requests related to allergies (アレルギー) and religious dietary restrictions; specifics of how these are handled in practice are not publicly documented.
Shojin ryori is structurally free of meat, fish, shellfish, and pungent alliums by religious tradition — a strong baseline for many vegan and plant-based diners.
The resident priest cultivates pesticide-free vegetables used in the meals, suggesting high ingredient integrity and intentional sourcing.
